dok_rationale: Part (c) adjudicates two incomplete normal-model claims by coordinating population shape, sample size, the 10 percent condition, sampling-distribution variability, and the consequence of rejecting a valid probability model.
stem: Suppose Lines A and B each contain 1{,}000 cycle times with population mean 40 seconds and standard deviation 12 seconds. Line A is approximately normal and is sampled with $n_A=9$; Line B is strongly right-skewed and is sampled with $n_B=36$. An auditor wants $P(\bar X>46)$ for each.\par\smallskip \textbf{Serena:} ``Only B can use a normal model because $36\geq30$; its probability is $0.00135$. A is too small.''\par \textbf{Mateo:} ``Only A can use a normal model because its population is normal; its probability is $0.0668$. B is too skewed.''
first_take: Which parts of Serena's and Mateo's reasoning look defensible? Cite one shape or sample-size detail.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the mean of each sampling distribution and the finite-population condition for using $\sigma_{\bar X}=\sigma/\sqrt n$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Verify the 10 percent condition, compute both sampling-distribution standard deviations, and calculate each normal tail probability when justified.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate both claims using population shape, sample size, the two normality pathways, and sampling variability. Determine which probabilities are warranted, explain any difference between them, and trace what each incomplete rule would cause the auditor to discard.

answers.a: Both sampling distributions have mean 40 seconds. Without replacement, each sample must be no more than 10 percent of its population to use $\sigma_{\bar X}=\sigma/\sqrt n$ without a finite-population correction.
answers.b: Both SRS sizes satisfy the cap $0.10(1{,}000)=100$. For A, $\sigma_{\bar X}=12/\sqrt9=4$; its normal population justifies $z=(46-40)/4=1.5$ and an upper tail of $0.0668$. For B, $\sigma_{\bar X}=12/\sqrt{36}=2$; the CLT applies because $36\geq30$, giving $z=3$ and an upper tail of $0.00135$.
answers.c: Neither whole claim is complete. Serena is right about B: despite population skew, $n_B=36$ activates the CLT and supports $0.00135$; she wrongly rejects A, whose normal population supports a normal sampling distribution at $n_A=9$. Mateo is right about A and $0.0668$ but ignores B's CLT route. Their rules would each discard one valid probability. Both models center at 40, but 46 is 1.5 sampling SDs above A's center and 3 above B's, so B's larger sample produces the smaller tail.

expectedElements.description: Concludes that both sampling distributions are approximately normal
Uses A's normal population and B's $n=36$ CLT route
Connects sampling SDs 4 and 2 to z-scores 1.5 and 3
Identifies the valid and invalid part of each claim
Explains that each incomplete rule discards a valid probability

scoringGuide.E: Validates both models with distinct routes, links variability to both tails, and diagnoses both exclusions.
scoringGuide.P: Recognizes both routes and probabilities but incompletely diagnoses a claim or the tail difference.
scoringGuide.I: Requires $n\geq30$ for a normal population, rejects the CLT for skew, or ignores sampling variability.
